details: Crew Vitals is a browser-based health monitoring tool for astronauts that turns daily check-ups into an interactive game. Each astronaut's health readings are taken on Earth before flight, and the tool then tracks eight indicators week by week: resting heart rate, blood oxygen, vision, wellbeing, sleep, bone density, leg strength and radiation dose. A 3D holographic body shows where each reading comes from. Instead of judging astronauts against one fixed Earth standard, the system compares each person with the past astronauts most similar to them, using their pre-flight readings and the environment they are in, whether a space station, a transit craft, the Moon, Mars or a surface rover. From those past crews it builds a personal "healthy for space" range, and its alerts focus on change rather than absolute values. It measures how surprising each week's change is compared with what was expected, catches slow drifts that build up over several weeks, and projects where a reading is heading so problems can be treated before they become critical, while fixed safety limits are always kept. The benefit is earlier, fairer and more personal warnings, because a reading that is normal for one astronaut in weightlessness may be a warning sign for another on Mars, and the intended impact is to support crews on long missions far from Earth, where help from doctors on the ground is delayed and astronauts must catch problems themselves. We built it in TypeScript with Three.js for the 3D scene, HTML, CSS and the Canvas API for the interface and charts, Vite for development and Vitest for automated tests of the health logic. It runs on any computer with a web browser and needs no special hardware, and we developed it with the help of an AI coding assistant. The project is creative because it combines a nearest-neighbour search on vectors built from health readings and environment hazards, statistical change detection and a game layer with experience points, streaks and missions into one tool that is easy to read at a glance through colour coding, while adapting its look and instructions to each environment. We considered the five hazards of spaceflight identified by NASA's Human Research Program (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity changes and closed environments), the risks they pose to the body and mind, how astronauts can realistically measure each indicator, and the need to keep absolute safety limits in place. The past astronaut data in this prototype is simulated, so the next step would be to connect it to real mission data.
